title: The infinitive and the participle in the sentence

objectives.can: Read an infinitive construct with its subject and object, an infinitive absolute, and a participle as predicate, attribute or noun.

explanation.summary: The two verbal nouns of Hebrew carry whole clauses. An infinitive construct with a preposition and a suffix often says 'when he …' or 'until they …'; the infinitive absolute strengthens a verb or stands in for one; and the participle can be a predicate, an attribute or a noun. This lesson shows how to read each in a sentence.

sections.heading: The infinitive construct with its subject and object
body: The infinitive construct has no person or tense. It names the action, and the grammar around it shows who does it and when. A preposition before it makes a clause: בְּ or כְּ with an infinitive means 'when', 'as' or 'as soon as'; עַד means 'until'; אַחֲרֵי means 'after'; מִן can mean 'from' (doing something) or 'so as not to'; and לְ often gives a purpose, as in the last lesson.

A suffix on the infinitive is most often its subject: בְּשֻׁבוֹ is 'when he returned', and בְּדַבְּרוֹ is 'when he spoke'. But a suffix can also be its object ('to deliver him'), and a reader tells them apart by the verb: an intransitive verb such as 'return' or 'stand' can only have the suffix as subject, and a transitive verb needs the context.

A noun can follow an infinitive as its subject, and a further noun as its object, which takes אֵת if it is definite: כִשְׁמֹעַ הָעָם אֶת קוֹל הַשּׁוֹפָר, 'when the people heard the sound of the horn'. The first noun after the infinitive is the subject, the second its object. The time of the clause is set by the main verb, before, at the same time or after.
Such a clause is frequently found after וַיְהִי, 'and it was', as a way of introducing the time of the next event. The infinitive clause is the time frame and the main event follows in a wayyiqtol.

sections.heading: The infinitive absolute
body: The infinitive absolute has three common jobs. Before a finite verb of the same root it strengthens the verb: מוֹת תָּמוּת is often rendered 'you shall surely die'. Grammarians describe the effect as emphasis, certainty or insistence, and they differ about how to put it; in a question such as הֲמָלֹךְ תִּמְלֹךְ it adds a note of challenge. Do not translate it the same way every time.

After a finite verb it shows a continuing or repeated action: הָלוֹךְ וָשׁוֹב is 'going and returning', and the waters 'receded continually'. And it can stand in the place of a finite verb altogether, in a command, as in שָׁמוֹר, 'keep!', or in a series of charges, as in 'will you steal, murder and commit adultery …?'. In these uses the person and the time must come from the context.

sections.heading: The participle as predicate
body: The participle can be the predicate of a clause: אַחֶיךָ רֹעִים, 'your brothers are shepherding'. As in the first lesson of this stage, the time comes from the context. With הִנֵּה it often marks something imminent. To say that something was going on over a stretch of the past, Hebrew often adds a form of הָיָה: הָיָה רֹעֶה, 'he was shepherding'; הָיוּ חֹרְשׁוֹת, 'they were ploughing'. The form of הָיָה gives the time and the participle the continuing action.
The participle agrees with its subject in gender and number. A feminine plural subject takes a feminine plural participle, as the oxen of Job 1:14 are matched with a feminine plural.

sections.heading: The participle as attribute and as noun
body: A participle can modify a noun, like an adjective, agreeing with it in gender, number and definiteness: 'the man who walks', 'the walking man'. Often it takes the article and is then like a relative clause: הַיֹּשֵׁב means 'the one who sits'. Without a noun to modify it works as a noun in its own right: a keeper, a shepherd, a killer.

A participle used as a noun can be in the construct state with a noun that stands for its object: יִרְאֵי אֱלֹהִים, 'fearers of God', 'those who fear God'. The second noun is the object of the action, and the chain has the force of a clause. Compare הֲשֹׁמֵר אָחִי אָנֹכִי, 'am I my brother's keeper?', where שֹׁמֵר is a noun-like participle with its object. Whether such a chain is better called a noun or a verb is one of the questions on which grammarians differ; the reader's task is to see who acts and who is acted upon.

head: Form
Pattern
Typical sense
rows: בְּ / כְּ + infinitive + suffix or noun
before a finite verb of the same root
after a finite verb, or alone
continuing action; a command or a charge
alone or with הָיָה as the predicate
with the article, or in construct with a noun
attribute, or a noun: 'the one who …', 'fearers of God'

misunderstandings: The suffix on an infinitive is not always the subject. With an intransitive verb it is; with a transitive verb it may be the object. Look at the verb.
The infinitive absolute does not simply mean 'surely'. It can strengthen a verb, continue an action, or take the place of a command. The context decides.
A participle is not a present tense. It can sit in a story as a past activity, in a speech as a present or a future, and in a law as a general statement.
A participle in construct with a noun is not a noun in the genitive in the ordinary sense: 'fearers of God' means those who fear God, with God as the object.

deeper.heading: Why the infinitive absolute is hard to describe
body: The infinitive absolute is not a verb with person and number, and it is not quite a noun either. Grammarians have called it an 'intensifying adverb', a 'verbal noun' and a 'verb-like absolute form'. The traditional account that it strengthens the verb is helpful, but it is only an account: in some places the same construction seems to concede a point, or to stress a contrast, rather than to make the statement stronger.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And Joseph was thirty years old when he stood before Pharaoh king of Egypt. — And Joseph went out from the presence of Pharaoh, and went throughout all the land of Egypt.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: בְּעָמְדוֹ is the infinitive construct of 'stand' with the prefix בְּ and the suffix 'he', the subject: 'when he stood'. The phrase before Pharaoh follows it. The clause fixes the time of Joseph's age; the main event comes with the wayyiqtol in the next clause.

quoted.title: Joshua
quoted.english: So the people shouted, and the priests blew with the horns. And it came to pass, when the people heard the sound of the horn, that the people shouted with a great shout, and the wall fell down flat, so that the people went up into the city, every man straight before him, and they took the city.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: After וַיְהִי a temporal clause with כְּ and an infinitive: כִשְׁמֹעַ הָעָם אֶת קוֹל הַשּׁוֹפָר. The noun הָעָם directly after the infinitive is its subject, and the definite object takes אֵת. The clause means 'when the people heard the sound of the horn' and gives the moment at which the main events follow.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: but of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, thou shalt not eat of it; for in the day that thou eatest thereof thou shalt surely die.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Two infinitives. בְּיוֹם אֲכָלְךָ is a temporal phrase with a construct infinitive and the suffix 'you' as subject: 'on the day of your eating'. מוֹת תָּמוּת has an infinitive absolute before a finite verb of the same root and is usually taken as an emphatic statement of certainty.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: These are the generations of Jacob. Joseph, being seventeen years old, was feeding the flock with his brethren, being still a lad even with the sons of Bilhah, and with the sons of Zilpah, his father's wives; and Joseph brought evil report of them unto their father.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: הָיָה with a participle: הָיָה רֹעֶה אֶת אֶחָיו בַּצֹּאן. The form of הָיָה puts the clause in the past, and the participle shows that the shepherding was going on. The participle takes the object marker like a verb, because it keeps the verb's government.

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: Moreover thou shalt provide out of all the people able men, such as fear God, men of truth, hating unjust gain; and place such over them, to be rulers of thousands, rulers of hundreds, rulers of fifties, and rulers of tens.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: Participles as nouns in the construct state. יִרְאֵי אֱלֹהִים is 'fearers of God' and שֹׂנְאֵי בָצַע is 'haters of gain'; each participle is plural construct, and the second noun is its object. They stand beside a plain construct, אַנְשֵׁי חַיִל, 'men of strength', in a list of the qualities of the men to be chosen.

quoted.title: 2 Samuel
quoted.english: And David got him a name when he returned from smiting the Arameans in the Valley of Salt, even eighteen thousand men.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: 'when he returned': a temporal clause with the suffix as subject
practice.explain: בְּ with an infinitive construct makes a temporal clause. The verb 'return' is intransitive, so the suffix can only be the subject: 'when he returned'.

practice.prompt: What is אַף אָחִיךָ (words 2 and 3) in 'עַד שׁוּב'?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: until thy brother's anger turn away from thee, and he forget that which thou hast done to him; then I will send, and fetch thee from thence; why should I be bereaved of you both in one day?'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: The subject of the infinitive: 'until your brother's anger turns away'
practice.explain: עַד with an infinitive means 'until', and the noun that follows is the subject of the action: the anger turns back. The verb is intransitive, so there is no object.

practice.prompt: What does the infinitive absolute הֲמָלֹךְ do before תִּמְלֹךְ (words 3 and 4)?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And his brethren said to him: 'Shalt thou indeed reign over us? or shalt thou indeed have dominion over us?' And they hated him yet the more for his dreams, and for his words.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It turns the verb into a noun
It strengthens the question, with a note of challenge: 'will you indeed reign?'
It makes the verb a command
practice.explain: An infinitive absolute of the same root before a finite verb strengthens it. Here the brothers sneer at the dream: 'Will you really be king over us?' The second half of the verse repeats the construction with מָשׁוֹל תִּמְשֹׁל.

practice.prompt: What does הָיוּ חֹרְשׁוֹת (words 6 and 7) express?

quoted.title: Job
quoted.english: that there came a messenger unto Job, and said: 'The oxen were plowing, and the asses feeding beside them;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: An activity that was going on in the past: the oxen were ploughing
A past event that finished at once
practice.explain: A form of הָיָה with a participle gives a continued action in the past. The participle is feminine plural to agree with 'oxen', and the plural form of הָיָה agrees too.

practice.prompt: What is רֹעִים (word 6) in this verse?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And Israel said unto Joseph: 'Do not thy brethren feed the flock in Shechem? come, and I will send thee unto them.' And he said to him: 'Here am I.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A finite verb in the qatal
A participle used as the predicate: 'your brothers are shepherding'
A noun in the construct state
practice.explain: The clause has no finite verb. The participle agrees with the plural subject אַחֶיךָ and gives the activity, and the phrase בִּשְׁכֶם gives the place. הֲלוֹא marks the question, expecting 'yes'.

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: If thou see the ass of him that hateth thee lying under its burden, thou shalt forbear to pass by him; thou shalt surely release it with him.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

practice.explain: מֵעֲזֹ֣ב is Qal, infinitive construct, infinitive, from עָזַב (leave, forsake).

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And they journeyed from Beth-el; and there was still some way to come to Ephrath; and Rachel travailed, and she had hard labour.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

practice.explain: בְּלִדְתָּֽהּ is Qal, infinitive construct, infinitive, from יָלַד (to bear, beget).

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: And they shall be upon Aaron, and upon his sons, when they go in unto the tent of meeting, or when they come near unto the altar to minister in the holy place; that they bear not iniquity, and die; it shall be a statute for ever unto him and unto his seed after him.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

practice.explain: בְּבֹאָ֣ם is Qal, infinitive construct, infinitive, from בּוֹא (to come, go in).

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And the king of Sodom went out to meet him, after his return from the slaughter of Chedorlaomer and the kings that were with him, at the vale of Shaveh — the same is the King's Vale.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

practice.explain: מֵֽהַכּוֹת֙ is Hiphil, infinitive construct, infinitive, from נָכָה (to strike, smite).

quoted.title: 2 Samuel
quoted.english: And it came to pass, when Joab kept watch upon the city, that he assigned Uriah unto the place where he knew that valiant men were.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

practice.explain: בִּשְׁמ֥וֹר is Qal, infinitive construct, infinitive, from שָׁמַר (to keep, watch).

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: And the LORD said unto Moses: 'Yet one plague more will I bring upon Pharaoh, and upon Egypt; afterwards he will let you go hence; when he shall let you go, he shall surely thrust you out hence altogether.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

practice.explain: כְּשַׁ֨לְּח֔וֹ is Piel, infinitive construct, infinitive, from שָׁלַח (to send, stretch out).

quoted.title: Joshua
quoted.english: And it came to pass, when the people removed from their tents, to pass over the Jordan, the priests that bore the ark of the covenant being before the people;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

practice.explain: בִּנְסֹ֤עַ is Qal, infinitive construct, infinitive, from נָסַע (pull out, up).

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: Moreover He said: 'I am the God of thy father, the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob.' And Moses hid his face; for he was afraid to look upon God.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

practice.explain: מֵהַבִּ֖יט is Hiphil, infinitive construct, infinitive, from נָבַט (look).

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And Abraham was ninety years old and nine, when he was circumcised in the flesh of his foreskin.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

practice.explain: בְּהִמֹּל֖וֹ is Niphal, infinitive construct, infinitive, from מוּל (circumcise, be circumcised).

quoted.title: Joshua
quoted.english: And it came to pass, when Joshua was by Jericho, that he lifted up his eyes and looked, and, behold, there stood a man over against him with his sword drawn in his hand; and Joshua went unto him, and said unto him: 'Art thou for us, or for our adversaries?'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

practice.explain: בִּֽהְי֣וֹת is Qal, infinitive construct, infinitive, from הָיָה (to be, become).

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: And the Egyptians shall know that I am the LORD, when I have gotten Me honour upon Pharaoh, upon his chariots, and upon his horsemen.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

practice.explain: בְּהִכָּבְדִ֣י is Niphal, infinitive construct, infinitive, from כָּבַד (be heavy, weighty).

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And it came to pass, when she saw that he had left his garment in her hand, and was fled forth,
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

practice.explain: כִּרְאוֹתָ֔הּ is Qal, infinitive construct, infinitive, from רָאָה (to see).

check.prompt: Who is the subject of the infinitive in כְּדַבְּרָהּ (word 1)?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And it came to pass, as she spoke to Joseph day by day, that he hearkened not unto her, to lie by her, or to be with her.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: The woman: the suffix 'she' is the subject, and אֶל יוֹסֵף says whom she spoke to
Joseph, who is named after it
No one; the infinitive has no subject
check.explain: כְּ with an infinitive gives 'as she spoke'. The suffix -ָהּ is the subject, and Joseph is the one addressed. The two infinitives with לְ at the end of the verse give what she asked him to do.

check.prompt: What does the infinitive absolute שָׁמוֹר (word 0) do at the head of this verse?

quoted.title: Deuteronomy
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It strengthens a finite verb that follows
It stands for a command, 'keep!', in place of an imperative
check.explain: No finite verb of the same root follows. The infinitive absolute stands alone and acts as a command; the sense of person and time comes from the context. The infinitive construct לְקַדְּשׁוֹ gives the aim, 'to keep it holy'.

check.prompt: How are the infinitives absolute in this verse used?

quoted.title: Jeremiah
quoted.english: Will ye steal, murder, and commit adultery, and swear falsely, and offer unto Baal, and walk after other gods whom ye have not known,
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: Each stands in the place of a finite verb in a series of charges put as a question
check.explain: The verse is a question introduced by ה, and its charges are infinitives absolute, with no finite verbs. The speaker lists the acts of which the people are accused: steal, murder, commit adultery.

check.prompt: What does the pair הָלוֹךְ וָשׁוֹב (words 4 and 5) add to וַיָּשֻׁבוּ?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And the waters returned from off the earth continually; and after the end of a hundred and fifty days the waters decreased.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It shows the action as continuing: the waters went on receding
It strengthens the verb in the manner of 'surely'
check.explain: Two infinitives absolute after a finite verb express a continuing or repeated movement, 'going and returning'. The English may say 'steadily' or 'continually'.

check.prompt: What do הָיוּ יְרֵאִים and הָיוּ עֹבְדִים (words 2, 3, 6, 7) describe?

quoted.title: 2 Kings
quoted.english: They feared the LORD, and served their own gods, after the manner of the nations from among whom they had been carried away.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: Two continued or habitual states in the past: they were fearing the LORD and serving their own gods
Two single events that took place long ago
check.explain: הָיָה with a participle, twice, describes what went on over a period. The participles are plural to agree with the subject, and both take their objects with אֵת.

check.prompt: What is יְרֵא אֱלֹהִים (words 14 and 15) in this speech?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And he said: 'Lay not thy hand upon the lad, neither do thou any thing unto him; for now I know that thou art a God-fearing man, seeing thou hast not withheld thy son, thine only son, from Me.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A participle (or verbal adjective) in the construct state with its object, 'one who fears God', and אַתָּה is the subject
A finite verb in the yiqtol
check.explain: The chain יְרֵא אֱלֹהִים is the predicate of a nominal clause: 'you (are) one fearing God'. God is the object of the fearing, and the chain is built like a construct.

check.prompt: What is שֹׁמֵר in הֲשֹׁמֵר אָחִי אָנֹכִי (words 10 to 12)?

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And the LORD said unto Cain: 'Where is Abel thy brother?' And he said: 'I know not; am I my brother's keeper?'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A participle used as a noun, 'keeper', followed by its object אָחִי and with אָנֹכִי as subject
check.explain: Cain answers with a question. The participle is the predicate: 'am I my brother's keeper?' The word that follows, אָחִי, is the object of the keeping, in the construct manner.

check.prompt: What is מַכֵּה אִישׁ (words 0 and 1) at the head of this law?

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: He that smiteth a man, so that he dieth, shall surely be put to death.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A finite verb followed by its subject
A participle as a noun, in construct with its object: 'one who strikes a man', the subject of the sentence
check.explain: The law names the offender by what he does. The participle is in construct with the noun that is the object of the striking, and the whole phrase is the subject; the answer מוֹת יוּמָת follows, with an infinitive absolute before the yiqtol.

check.prompt: What does מִמְּלֹךְ עֲלֵיהֶם (word 18 onward) say?

quoted.title: 1 Samuel
quoted.english: And the LORD said unto Samuel: 'Hearken unto the voice of the people in all that they say unto thee; for they have not rejected thee, but they have rejected Me, that I should not be king over them.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: 'from being king over them': they rejected the LORD so that he should not reign over them
check.explain: מִן with an infinitive construct can give the thing from which one turns away or the end that is kept off. The reading 'that I should not be king over them' takes the clause as the effect or aim of the rejection.

check.prompt: What is the suffix in חֲיוֹתָם (word 10)?

quoted.title: Joshua
quoted.english: And it came to pass, when all the nation were circumcised, every one of them, that they abode in their places in the camp, till they were whole.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: The subject of the infinitive: 'until they were whole (recovered)'
A possessive on a noun, 'their lives'
check.explain: עַד with an infinitive and a suffix gives a clause of time, 'until their recovering'. The verb חָיָה is intransitive here, so the suffix is the subject.

check.prompt: What is the relation between בְּרִדְתּוֹ and בְּדַבְּרוֹ אִתּוֹ (words 10 and 20 to 21)?

quoted.title: Exodus
quoted.english: And it came to pass, when Moses came down from mount Sinai with the two tables of the testimony in Moses' hand, when he came down from the mount, that Moses knew not that the skin of his face sent forth beams while He talked with him.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: The first is a noun, the second a verb
Both are temporal infinitives with a suffix as subject: 'when he came down' and 'when he spoke with him'
check.explain: The verse piles up בְּ + infinitive clauses (בְּרֶדֶת, בְּרִדְתּוֹ, בְּדַבְּרוֹ) to set the time of Moses's not knowing. In each the suffix or the noun after it is the subject.

reading.why: The story of Joseph and his brothers opens with הָיָה and a participle in verse 2, and in verse 8 the brothers answer his dream with two infinitives absolute before finite verbs. The passage shows two of the jobs the verbal nouns do in a sentence.
